say.text: A 35-year-old woman comes to you with bloody discharge from one duct of the breast. Nothing is palpable.
Predict first: what is the most common cause?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Intraductal papilloma is the commonest cause of bloody discharge from a single duct.
Carcinoma still has to be excluded. Retraction, bloody discharge and eczema-like change are the nipple signs that need a work-up.
That is not the right choice: bloody discharge is the alarming sign, so carcinoma feels like the commonest cause.
Frequency and danger are different questions, and this stem asks for the commonest cause.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the qualifier in the stem: 'most common' asks how often, not how worrying.

say.text: Ask two questions separately: which cause occurs most often at 35, and which cause you must still rule out.
Bloody discharge from one duct is most often an intraductal papilloma. Carcinoma is the cause you must exclude, not the one that occurs most.
Eczema-like change that starts at the nipple and spreads to the areola is Paget's disease, which is one of the nipple signs to work up.
A 50-year-old woman has a 3 cm tumour in the breast. Peau d'orange lies over it, with no redness or warmth.
Which T category does this give?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Peau d'orange comes from blocked skin lymphatics with oedema, and that places the tumour in T4b.
The size of the lump does not change this T4 category.
That is not the right choice: the orange-peel skin sign looks dramatic, so it feels like the whole inflammatory picture.
One skin sign is not the same as the clinical picture of the disease. Look at the whole breast before you name the category.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck whether the whole breast is red, warm and swollen before naming inflammatory disease.

say.text: Ask whether the whole breast looks inflamed, or whether one patch of skin over the tumour is involved.
Peau d'orange alone is skin involvement, so the tumour is T4b, whatever its size.
T4d needs the whole picture: a red, warm, swollen breast with peau d'orange over at least one-third of it, often with no discrete lump.
Two women each have a new breast lump. One is 28 and one is 52.
Which imaging suits each of them?

choices.label: Ultrasound for the 28-year-old, mammography for the 52-year-old
Mammography for both women, the screening test
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Under about 35 the breast is dense, and ultrasound is preferred there. It also separates solid from cystic lesions.
Mammography is the screening tool of choice over about 35 to 40.
That is not the right choice: mammography is the test everyone knows, so it feels right for any breast lump.
Screening tests carry an age range, and each woman's age decides the first imaging.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age first, before the test you know best.

say.text: Take each woman's age separately. What does her breast tissue look like at that age?
Ultrasound is preferred in women under 35 and in dense breasts, and it distinguishes solid from cystic lesions.
Mammography is the screening tool of choice and the main imaging test in women over about 35 to 40.
A team plans neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a breast mass. They need invasive or in-situ status, plus ER, PR and HER2 status.
Which sample do you send?

choices.label: Fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass
Core needle biopsy of the mass
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A core needle sample gives histology, so invasive and in-situ disease can be told apart.
The same sample also reports grade and ER, PR and HER2 status.
That is not the right choice: cytology of a breast lump is the test older papers expect, so it feels safe.
Loose cells on a slide do not show the tissue architecture the team is asking about.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the pathologist must report before you name the sample.

say.text: List what the team must get back from the pathologist: invasion, grade and receptors, or only whether cells are present.
Older papers expected FNAC for a breast lump. Current practice is core needle biopsy, which gives histology and receptor status.
FNAC is kept mainly for axillary nodes and cysts.
A 38-year-old has a 1.5 cm invasive ductal carcinoma on core biopsy. Her nodes are clinically negative and she has no symptoms.
What do you order next for distant spread?

choices.label: No routine distant-spread scan; plan local treatment
Whole-body bone scan to exclude spread first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Routine distant-spread imaging is not needed in early, asymptomatic disease.
It is done for locally advanced disease or symptoms. Early disease goes to local treatment first.
That is not the right choice: bone is the commonest site of spread, so a bone scan feels like routine work-up.
Where metastases usually go does not tell you who needs a scan. Stage and symptoms do.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the stage and symptoms before ordering any distant-spread test.

say.text: Ask what this patient's stage and symptoms would make you look for, not what a scan could find.
CT chest and abdomen, bone scan or PET-CT are done for locally advanced disease or symptoms.
CA 15-3 and CEA monitor known metastatic disease. They do not screen or stage.
Last check on this breast work-up, across the lump, the imaging and the spread scans.
Which three arms make up triple assessment?

choices.label: Clinical examination, imaging and fine needle aspiration
Clinical examination, imaging and tissue diagnosis
Clinical examination, mammography and bone scan
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Triple assessment is clinical examination, imaging and tissue diagnosis.
Most breast cancers present as a painless, hard, irregular lump with ill-defined margins.
That is not the right choice: a bone scan feels like part of the work-up, because spread is the feared outcome.
Triple assessment is about the breast itself. Distant spread is staged only when stage or symptoms call for it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the spread scan belongs to the breast arms or to staging.

say.text: That is not the right choice: imaging and a needle sample feel like a complete breast work-up.
A needle that gives loose cells does not replace a tissue diagnosis when the team needs histology and receptors.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which arm gives histology before you accept the needle.

say.text: Name the three arms by what each one does: examine, image, and take tissue for histology.
Triple assessment is clinical examination, imaging and tissue diagnosis, and core needle biopsy is the tissue test.
Bone scans belong to staging for locally advanced disease or symptoms, not to the breast arms.
MRI is the most sensitive imaging test. It is used to judge the extent of invasive lobular carcinoma.
Invasive lobular carcinoma is the type most often bilateral or multicentric, so its extent matters before surgery.
